Car Insurance Claim Prediction

A comprehensive end-to-end machine learning project for predicting whether a car insurance policyholder will file a claim — built with Python, Flask & Streamlit.
IBM AICTE AI/ML Internship Project  |  Dataset: 10,000 records · 18 features
Best Model: Gradient Boosting  |  Accuracy: 84.25%  |  ROC-AUC: 0.9125

1. Project Overview

Car insurance companies face significant financial risk from fraudulent or high-frequency claims. Predicting whether a policyholder will file a claim — before it happens — allows insurers to price risk accurately, prioritise underwriting reviews, and intervene proactively with high-risk customers.

This project builds a production-ready binary classification pipeline that takes 17 policyholder attributes and outputs a claim probability, a prediction label, and a risk tier (Low / Medium / High). The system consists of three independent layers:

  • train_model.py — data ingestion, preprocessing, multi-model training, auto-selection, artefact export
  • app.py — Flask REST API exposing POST /predict and GET /stats
  • streamlit_app.py — Streamlit web UI with a Predict page and an Analytics Dashboard

3. Dataset Insights & Exploratory Data Analysis

EDA was performed across all 17 features to understand distributions, correlations with the target variable, and key risk signals. The following charts and insights were derived directly from the dataset.

3.1 — Demographic Risk Factors

Fig 2 — Claim rate drops sharply as driver age increases
Fig 3 — Male drivers file claims at a higher rate than female drivers

🔴 Highest Risk Age: 16–25

Young drivers (16–25) have a claim rate of 71.8% — nearly 3× that of 65+ drivers (9.8%). Inexperience and risk-taking behaviour are primary contributing factors.

🟡 Gender Difference

Male drivers: 36.3% claim rate vs. female drivers: 26.4%. This is consistent with broader industry data showing higher risk propensity in male drivers.

3.2 — Driving Behaviour Risk Factors

Fig 4 — Claim rate falls steadily with years of driving experience
Fig 5 — Claim filers (red) cluster at higher speeding violations and past accidents

🔴 Experience is the Strongest Predictor

Drivers with 0–9 years experience have a claim rate of 62.8% vs. 1.9% for 30+ year veterans. Experience is the single most discriminating demographic feature.

🟡 Violations & Accidents Compound Risk

Speeding violations and past accidents are strongly correlated with claims. Policyholders with 5+ violations have a claim rate over 2× the dataset average, confirming these as critical underwriting signals.

3.3 — Socioeconomic Risk Factors

Fig 6 — Lower income classes file claims at significantly higher rates
Fig 7 — Claim filers (red) tend to have lower credit scores

🔴 Income-Claim Correlation

Poverty-level income drivers show a claim rate of 65.4% compared to upper class at 13.4%. Lower income may correlate with older vehicles, deferred maintenance, and higher financial stress.

🟢 Credit Score as Risk Proxy

Higher credit scores correlate with lower claim probability. Policyholders who did not file claims have a mean credit score of 0.546 vs. 0.45 for claim filers. Credit score is a strong continuous risk signal.

3.4 — Vehicle Risk Factors

Fig 8 — Sports cars have a higher claim rate than sedans

🟣 Sports Cars = Higher Risk

Sports car drivers have a claim rate of 32.5% vs. 31.3% for sedan owners. Higher speeds and performance characteristics correlate with increased accident probability.

🟡 Vehicle Age Impact

Vehicles manufactured before 2015 have a claim rate of 40.3% vs. 10.6% for post-2015 models. Older vehicles may lack modern safety features, contributing to higher claim frequency.

Key EDA Summary: The top claim risk signals are (1) young age + low driving experience, (2) poverty/working-class income, (3) low credit score, (4) 2+ speeding violations or past accidents, and (5) sports car vehicle type. These align with the feature importance rankings produced by the trained model.

4.1 — Algorithm: Gradient Boosting

Gradient Boosting is an ensemble learning method that builds decision trees sequentially, where each tree corrects the errors of its predecessor. It optimises a differentiable loss function (log-loss for classification) using gradient descent in function space. Key properties:

  • n_estimators = 150 — number of boosting rounds (trees built)
  • learning_rate (default 0.1) — shrinkage factor applied to each tree's contribution
  • max_depth (default 3) — maximum depth of individual trees
  • Subsample (default 1.0) — fraction of samples used for each tree
  • random_state = 42 — ensures reproducibility

4.2 — Model Selection Process

Three classifiers were trained and compared. The winner was selected automatically by highest 5-fold cross-validated ROC-AUC on the training set.

ModelTest AccuracyCV-AUC (5-fold)Test AUCSelected
Logistic Regression83.30%0.90720.8925—
Random Forest (150 trees)82.75%0.90630.8919—
Gradient Boosting 84.25% 0.9239 0.9125 ✅ BEST
Gradient Boosting was selected because it achieved the highest test AUC (0.9125) and CV-AUC (0.9239), indicating both strong discriminative ability and reliable generalisation to unseen data. The gap between CV-AUC and test AUC is only 0.0114, confirming minimal overfitting.

✅ Strong No-Claim Performance

The model identifies No Claim policyholders with 89.0% precision and 88.0% recall (F1: 0.885). Out of 1373 actual no-claim cases, 1208 were correctly identified.

⚠️ Claim Detection Trade-off

For the Claim class (minority), the model achieves 76.1% recall and 74.3% precision (F1: 0.752). Of 627 actual claims, 150 were missed (false negatives). This is acceptable for insurance pricing use-cases where some false negatives are tolerated over excessive false positives.

6. Business Insights

The model's predictions and feature importances translate directly into actionable underwriting and pricing intelligence. The following insights are derived from the model's behaviour on the dataset.

🚨 Young + Inexperienced = Highest Risk Segment

Policyholders aged 16–25 with <10 years experience represent the highest-risk demographic. Their claim rate (71.8%) is more than double the dataset average (31.3%). This segment warrants higher premiums, mandatory telematics, or graduated coverage structures.

🚨 Violations Are a Compounding Risk Signal

Each additional speeding violation and DUI offence significantly increases predicted claim probability. Policyholders with 2+ violations should be flagged for manual underwriting review or surcharge pricing. The model weights these features heavily.

💡 Credit Score as a Pricing Variable

Credit score (mean 0.516) is the 2nd most important feature. Insurers in jurisdictions where credit-based insurance scoring is permitted can directly incorporate this into actuarial rate tables. A score below 0.4 correlates with claim rates nearly 2× the average.

💡 Sports Car Surcharge is Justified

Sports car drivers show a claim rate of 32.5% vs. 31.3% for sedans. The model identifies vehicle type as a material risk factor, supporting a structured premium surcharge for high-performance vehicles.

✅ Long-Experience Drivers = Low-Risk, Price-Competitive Segment

Drivers with 30+ years experience have a claim rate of just 1.9%. Offering lower premiums to this segment would be actuarially sound and could be used as a competitive differentiator to attract low-risk, profitable policyholders.

✅ Vehicle Ownership Reduces Risk

Policyholders who own their vehicles (VEHICLE_OWNERSHIP = 1) tend to exercise more care and have lower claim rates. This "skin in the game" effect can be incorporated into pricing models as a discount factor for owned-vehicle policies.

ROC-AUC = 0.9125: The model correctly ranks a randomly selected claim policyholder above a randomly selected non-claim policyholder 91.2% of the time. This is significantly better than random (50%) and represents strong commercial utility for risk segmentation and portfolio management.

7. Business Analysis

7.1 — Problem Statement & Commercial Context

Car insurance is a data-intensive, risk-priced product. Insurers that can accurately predict which policyholders are likely to file claims gain a structural competitive advantage: they can price risk more accurately, reduce adverse selection, and deploy capital more efficiently. This model directly addresses that need.

7.2 — Risk Segmentation Matrix

SegmentProfileClaim RateModel OutputRecommended Action
HIGH RISK Age 16–25, 0–9y exp, poverty income, 2+ violations ~52–65% Probability >65% Premium surcharge + telematics requirement
MEDIUM RISK Age 26–39, 10–19y exp, working class, 1 violation ~25–40% Probability 40–65% Standard pricing + annual review
LOW RISK Age 40+, 20y+ exp, middle/upper class, 0 violations ~10–20% Probability <40% Preferred pricing + loyalty discount

7.3 — Financial Impact Estimate

Using the test set of 2,000 records as a proxy for a portfolio of 2,000 policyholders:

Total claims in test set627 Baseline exposure without model
Claims correctly flagged (TP)477 Early intervention possible for 477 cases
Claims missed (FN)150 Unavoidable exposure — model limitation
False alarms (FP)165 Unnecessary review cost for 165 customers
Correctly cleared (TN)1208 Efficient processing of 1208 low-risk policies
Claim detection rate76.1% Of every 100 claims, model flags 76.1

7.4 — Use-Case Applications

📋 Underwriting Decision Support

Underwriters can query the API with a new applicant's profile to get an instant risk score. High-probability applicants (>65%) are automatically routed for manual review, reducing workload for the remaining 70%+ of standard cases.

💰 Dynamic Premium Pricing

The model's probability output (0–100%) provides a continuous risk score that can replace or supplement actuarial rate tables. Premiums can be directly proportional to predicted claim probability, enabling more granular pricing.

🛡️ Fraud & Anomaly Flagging

When a low-probability policyholder (model predicts <20%) files a claim, the contrast triggers an anomaly flag. This is a lightweight proxy for claims fraud detection with no additional modelling required.

📊 Portfolio Risk Monitoring

Running the model monthly across the full active policy book generates a risk distribution. Sudden shifts in aggregate risk score can signal portfolio deterioration early — enabling reserve adjustments before claims materialise.

7.5 — Model Limitations

  • Synthetic dataset: The dataset is simulated. Real-world performance may differ once deployed on live insurance data with different distributions.
  • Class imbalance: With 31.3% claims, the model has lower precision on the positive class (74%). In production, threshold tuning may be needed to optimise for FP vs FN trade-offs.
  • Feature scope: The model lacks claim severity data (claim amount), policy history, telematics data, and geographic risk scores — all of which would improve accuracy.
  • Temporal drift: The model is a static snapshot. As driving patterns, vehicle technology, and regulations evolve, the model requires periodic retraining.
  • Fairness considerations: Features like RACE and GENDER introduce potential fairness concerns. Regulatory review of permissible rating factors is required before production deployment.

8. User Interface — Predict Page

The Streamlit frontend runs on localhost:8501. The Predict page collects all 17 input features through a structured form, serialises them as JSON, and sends them to the Flask POST /predict endpoint. The API response is rendered immediately below the form with full risk context.

10. System Architecture

Architecture: Streamlit (port 8501) → HTTP POST/GET → Flask REST API (port 5000) → model.pkl. The frontend and backend are fully decoupled. Any client (browser, mobile app, curl) can call the Flask API directly without the Streamlit layer.

12. Future Scope

The current system provides a solid production-grade baseline. The following enhancements are prioritised by expected impact and implementation feasibility.

12.1 — Model Improvements

🧠 Advanced Ensemble Methods

Replace single Gradient Boosting with XGBoost / LightGBM / CatBoost for faster training, native categorical handling, and GPU acceleration. Expected AUC improvement: +0.01 to +0.03.

🔧 Hyperparameter Optimisation

Apply Optuna or Bayesian Optimisation to tune n_estimators, learning_rate, max_depth, subsample, and min_samples_leaf. Current model uses scikit-learn defaults beyond n_estimators=150.

⚖️ Class Imbalance Handling

Apply SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Oversampling) or class_weight='balanced' to improve recall on the minority claim class. Target: push claim recall from 76% to 82%+ without degrading precision below 70%.

📊 Threshold Optimisation

Instead of the default 0.5 decision threshold, tune the classification threshold using the Precision-Recall curve to find the optimal operating point for the specific cost ratio of false positives vs false negatives in insurance.

12.2 — Feature Engineering

📡 Telematics Integration

Integrate real-time telematics data (hard braking events, night driving %, average speed, acceleration patterns) from IoT devices. These usage-based insurance (UBI) signals are the strongest predictors of claims in modern actuarial models.

🗺️ Geospatial Risk Scoring

Replace the raw POSTAL_CODE with area-level risk scores: accident frequency per km², road quality index, weather risk index, and urban vs rural classification. Geospatial features typically improve model AUC by 1–3%.

📅 Policy History Features

Add claim history features: number of prior claims, years as a customer, premium payment punctuality, and policy renewal count. Retention signals are strongly correlated with claim behaviour.

💲 Claim Severity Prediction

Extend from binary classification (will claim?) to regression (how much will the claim cost?). A two-stage model — first predict claim likelihood, then predict severity conditional on a claim — enables expected loss pricing.

12.3 — System & Infrastructure Improvements

🐳 Dockerised Deployment

Containerise Flask API and Streamlit app as separate Docker containers orchestrated with docker-compose. Enables one-command deployment on any cloud provider (AWS ECS, Azure Container Apps, GCP Cloud Run).

🔄 MLflow / MLOps Pipeline

Integrate MLflow for experiment tracking, model versioning, and automated model registry. Add scheduled retraining with data drift detection (evidently AI or Alibi Detect) to trigger retraining when feature distributions shift.

🔒 API Authentication & Rate Limiting

Add JWT-based API authentication, request rate limiting, and input validation middleware to the Flask API before production deployment. Currently the API has no auth — appropriate only for internal/demo use.

📈 Real-Time Monitoring Dashboard

Build a Grafana + Prometheus monitoring layer to track API latency, prediction distribution drift, request volume, and error rates in real time. Add alerting when claim probability distribution shifts by >5% week-over-week.

12.4 — Explainability & Fairness

🔍 SHAP Explanations

Integrate SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to generate per-prediction explanation reports. Each API response would include a ranked list of features that most influenced the prediction — critical for regulatory compliance (e.g., adverse action notices under FCRA/ECOA).

⚖️ Fairness Auditing

Run AI Fairness 360 (IBM) or Fairlearn audits to measure disparate impact across protected attributes (RACE, GENDER) before any production deployment. Ensure Equal Opportunity and Demographic Parity constraints are met or documented.

Recommended Next Steps (Priority Order): (1) Threshold optimisation for better FN/FP trade-off → (2) SHAP integration for explainability → (3) LightGBM replacement for performance → (4) Docker deployment for scalability → (5) Telematics feature ingestion for accuracy uplift
